implementation_notes: Boost.Asio supplies the machinery but not the bookkeeping: io_context drives completion, async_write/async_read carry the request and the reply, and a steady_timer (monotonic clock) provides the deadline. With one outstanding request per connection the socket pair is the reply channel; with several the application adds the classic request-id -> completion-handler table. The completion handler must be guarded so that read completion and timer expiry can only settle the call once. Prefer this form when the protocol is yours; gRPC or ZeroMQ replace the whole exchange when they fit.
pitfalls: A cancelled timer's handler still runs with boost::asio::error::operation_aborted, so the request completion must be guarded to settle exactly once.
The socket, buffers and completion state must outlive the async chain (shared_ptr/shared_from_this); lambdas capturing stack locals are the classic dangling bug.
Blocking work inside an io_context handler stalls every other completion on that thread, including deadline timers.

variants.name: Boost.Asio awaitable with a C++20 timer race
variants.implementation_notes: C++20 coroutines let the exchange be written as linear code: the request is an awaitable, the deadline is another awaitable, and Asio's experimental awaitable_operators race them with || so that the loser is cancelled - the reply channel is the coroutine's completion and cancellation is Asio's per-operation cancellation state. Choose it when the toolchain is C++20 and the callback form obscures the timeout logic; the operators are experimental, so pin the Boost version.
pitfalls: awaitable_operators is experimental and has changed between Boost releases - pin the version and re-test on upgrade.
The losing operation is cancelled, but its side effects on the socket are not rolled back: reset or close the connection before reusing it.

variants.name: gRPC unary call with a propagated deadline
variants.implementation_notes: gRPC makes a unary RPC the unit of request-reply: the generated stub returns the response or a Status, the HTTP/2 stream is the reply channel and the stream itself is the correlation, so no message identifier is needed. ClientContext::set_deadline propagates the deadline to the server and cancels the call on expiry, and the Status carries the domain error. Use it when both ends can adopt protobuf and a service definition; the cost is generated code, a build-system dependency and an IDL workflow.
pitfalls: set_deadline takes a system_clock time point, so an NTP adjustment can shorten or extend it, and the server-side handler may keep working unless it observes context cancellation.
The synchronous API blocks one thread per call; use the async API or a CompletionQueue when call volume is high.
